hints: Find the longest chain that contains the $C=C$ bond and number it so the double bond gets the lowest possible number.
walkthrough:
Find the parent chain through the double bond**
Look at $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$. The longest continuous chain containing the $C=C$ is 6 carbons long, so the parent is hexene.

Number to give the double bond the lowest locant**
Numbering from the right gives the double bond at carbon 2, so it is hex-2-ene. The methyl branch is then on carbon 4, giving 4-methylhex-2-ene.

hints: Think about what stays the same and what changes: connectivity versus arrangement in space.
walkthrough:
Separate connectivity from geometry**
Stereoisomers are not structural isomers. The atoms are joined in the same order, so they have the same structural formula. What is different is how those groups point in three dimensional space.
Final answer: Compounds with the same structural formula but with a different arrangement of atoms or groups in space.

hints: Check the $C=C$ bond first: does each doubly bonded carbon carry two different groups?
Look away from the double bond for a carbon with four different groups attached.
Recall how one cis-trans pair and one chiral centre each multiply the number of isomers.
Combine the two independent sources of stereoisomerism to state the total number.
walkthrough:
Test for cis-trans isomerism**
Look at $\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$ on the right and $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ on the left of the double bond. On the left $C$, the groups are $H$ and a branched alkyl group. On the right $C$, the groups are $H$ and $\text{CH}_3$. Because each $C$ of the $C=C$ has two different groups and rotation is restricted by the pi bond, cis-trans isomerism is possible. That gives 2 isomers.

Test for optical isomerism**
Now look at carbon 4, $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)(\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3)$. It is bonded to $H$, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$. Those are four different groups, so it is a chiral centre. A chiral centre gives a pair of non-superimposable mirror images, so 2 optical isomers.

Combine the two effects**
These are independent. Each cis or trans form can exist as either optical isomer. So $2 \times 2 = 4$ stereoisomers in total.

Final answer: There are 4 stereoisomers.
Cis-trans (E-Z) isomerism about the $C=C$ double bond because each double-bonded carbon has two different groups attached.
Optical isomerism due to one chiral carbon centre, the $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)(\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3)$ carbon bonded to four different groups.
2 cis-trans isomers x 2 optical isomers = 4 in total.

hints: Identify the longest chain through the $C=C$ and count the methyl substituents on each doubly bonded carbon.
walkthrough:
Name the symmetrical alkene**
For $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ the longest chain through the double bond is 4 carbons, so but-2-ene. There is one methyl on C2 and one methyl on C3, giving 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene.

hints: Recall what cold, dilute, acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$ does to a $C=C$ bond compared with hot, concentrated conditions.
walkthrough:
Add two OH groups across the double bond**
Cold, dilute, acidified manganate(VII) gives mild oxidation. The pi bond breaks and an $\text{OH}$ adds to each $C$ of the former $C=C$. So $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ becomes $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C(OH)}-\text{C(OH)}(\text{CH}_3)_2$, which is 2,3-dimethylbutane-2,3-diol. In skeletal form show the central $C-C$ with two $\text{OH}$ groups and methyl branches.
Final answer: 2,3-dimethylbutane-2,3-diol: $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C(OH)C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)}_2$, with an $\text{OH}$ group added to each of the two central carbons, drawn in skeletal form.

hints: Think of hot, concentrated $\text{MnO}_4^-$ as cutting the $C=C$ completely and turning each doubly bonded carbon into a carbonyl.
walkthrough:
Cleave the double bond to carbonyls**
Hot, concentrated, acidified manganate(VII) cleaves the $C=C$ bond. Each $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=$ fragment becomes $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C}=\text{O}$. That molecule is propanone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$. Two moles form per mole of alkene.
Final answer: Propanone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$

hints: Remember addition polymerisation opens the $C=C$ to a $C-C$ single bond and joins many monomers head to tail.
walkthrough:
Build the saturated backbone**
In addition polymerisation the double bond in $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ opens to give the repeat unit $-\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_2-\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_2-$. Draw three of these joined in a chain with $C-C$ single bonds, methyl groups on every backbone carbon, and continuation bonds through the ends to show exactly three repeat units.

Final answer: -$\text{[C(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{]}_3$- shown with single bonds in the backbone, continuation bonds at each end, and exactly three repeat units: -$\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_2$-

hints: Find the longest chain containing the $C=C$ and number from the end closest to the double bond.
walkthrough:
Name the three carbon alkene**
For $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$ the parent chain is 3 carbons with the double bond starting at C1, so prop-1-ene. With a methyl on C2, the name is 2-methylprop-1-ene, commonly called methylpropene.
Final answer: 2-methylprop-1-ene (methylpropene)

hints: Start by polarising $\text{H-Br}$ and thinking about which atom the electron rich $C=C$ will attack.
Recall that the $C=C$ pi electrons form the new $C-H$ bond while the $\text{H-Br}$ bond electrons go to bromine.
Decide which carbon gets the $H$ to give the more stable carbocation intermediate.
Finish by showing how the bromide ion attacks the positively charged carbon.
walkthrough:
Attack by the alkene on the electrophile**
$\text{H-Br}$ is polarised $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ because $Br$ is more electronegative. The $C=C$ is electron rich. Draw a curly arrow from the $C=C$ pi bond to the $\text{H}^{\delta+}$, and a second curly arrow from the $\text{H-Br}$ bond onto $Br$ to give $\text{Br}^-$. Show partial charges and the lone pairs on $Br$.

Form the most stable carbocation**
The $H$ adds to the $\text{CH}_2$ carbon so the positive charge lands on the more substituted carbon, giving the tertiary carbocation $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C}^+$. Draw this ion in the box with the positive charge on the central carbon.

Capture of the carbocation by bromide**
Now draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{:Br}^-$ to the $\text{C}^+$ to form the $C-Br$ bond, giving $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CBr}$, which is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (labelled as 2-bromomethylpropane in the paper).

Final answer: Step 1: curly arrow from $C=C$ to $\text{H}^{\delta+}$ of $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$; curly arrow from $\text{H-Br}$ bond to $\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ to form $\text{Br}^-$.
Intermediate: tertiary carbocation $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C}^+$, $\text{H}_3\text{C-C}^+\text{(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_3$.
Step 2: curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{:Br}^-$ to $\text{C}^+$ to give $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CBr}$, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

hints: Compare the two possible carbocations: one with the charge on a tertiary carbon and one with the charge on a primary carbon.
Think about how methyl groups push electron density toward a neighbouring positive charge.
Link greater electron donation to lower charge density and lower energy, hence faster formation.
walkthrough:
Identify the competing intermediates**
If $H$ adds to the $\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_2$ end you get a primary carbocation. If $H$ adds to the $\text{CH}_2$ end you get a tertiary carbocation, $\text{C}^+$ bonded to three carbons. The product ratio is decided by which carbocation forms more easily.

Use the inductive effect to compare stability**
Methyl groups are electron releasing. Three methyl groups push more electron density toward the $\text{C}^+$ than one methyl group does. This positive inductive effect spreads out and reduces the concentrated positive charge density on carbon.

Connect stability to major product**
Lower charge density means lower energy and greater stability. The tertiary ion is therefore much more stable and forms faster, so almost all molecules go through that route to give 2-bromomethylpropane, with only small amounts going via the unstable primary ion to 1-bromomethylpropane.

Final answer: The tertiary carbocation intermediate is more stable than the primary carbocation.
Three methyl groups exert a positive inductive (electron donating) effect compared with only one methyl group for the primary route.
This reduces the positive charge density on the $\text{C}^+$, stabilising it, so the tertiary pathway predominates giving 2-bromomethylpropane as the major product.
